sections.html:
The Bernalillo County Clerk's Recording and Filing department takes deeds, mortgages, liens, judgments and plats. It sits at Alvarado Square, 415 Silver Ave SW in Albuquerque. Call 505-468-1290 or write to clerk@bernco.gov.

The county is New Mexico's most populous, with more than 676,000 residents, and about 106,000 of them live outside city limits. Whether a house is in Albuquerque, Los Ranchos, Tijeras or the unincorporated area, its deed goes through this one office.

Counter hours are Monday to Friday, 8 a.m. to 5 p.m., with a lunch closure from noon to 1:15 p.m. The public access area, where you can search records yourself for free, runs 8 a.m. to 4:45 p.m.

sections.h2: What the clerk requires before recording a deed
sections.html:
The clerk needs the original document, signed and notarized, with the notary's stamp or seal and the full legal description of the property. A court document must be a certified copy bearing the court's stamp or seal. Bring or send:

  • The original document, not a photocopy.
  • Signature and notarization, with the notary's seal and expiration date if there is one.
  • The full legal description of the Bernalillo County property.
  • The $25 recording fee, paid to BERNALILLO COUNTY.
  • A stamped, self-addressed envelope if you file by mail.

Clerk staff cannot give legal advice. They won't supply a form, explain how to fill one out or confirm you picked the right one, so have a title company, attorney or escrow officer draft the deed before it arrives.

Once recorded, a document is public and anyone can read it. The clerk redacts taxpayer ID numbers, financial account numbers, driver's license numbers, Social Security numbers and dates of birth, leaving only the last four digits or the year.

Recording is $25 per document for up to 10 entries, plus another $25 for each additional group of 10 or fewer. The county takes every payment method except American Express.

ServiceFee
Record a document (up to 10 entries)$25
Each additional group of 10 entries or fewer$25
Copy, not certified$1 per page
Certified copy$2 per document, plus $1 per page
Electronic copy, emailed$1 per page
Faxed copy$2 plus the copy fee
Plat copy, 8.5 by 11 or 11 by 17 inches$1 per page

The clerk's fee schedule is made up of recording and copy charges and has no transfer tax line. On the clerk's side, a deed transfer costs the $25 recording fee plus any copies you order. Title, escrow and attorney charges are billed separately.

sections.h2: Can a deed be recorded electronically or by mail?
sections.html:
Yes to both. You can file in person with cash, card or check, mail the original to the clerk, or have a third-party vendor submit it electronically.

Mail goes to Bernalillo County Clerk's Office, Attn: Recording and Filing, P.O. Box 542, Albuquerque, NM 87103-0542. For electronic filing, the clerk works with five eRecording vendors: Kuvera Enterprise Solutions, Affiliated Computer Services, CSC eRecording Solutions, USA Digital Solutions and Simplifile. eRecording isn't meant for individuals, and the vendor list is not an endorsement. A title or escrow company usually handles this step for you.

If you go in person, parking is free at 5th and Silver, with metered street parking nearby.

sections.h2: Assessor affidavit after a residential sale
sections.html:
New Mexico adds a second filing. Under section 7-38-12.1 NMSA 1978, a residential deed presented for recording must be followed by an affidavit filed with the county assessor within 30 days of the date the clerk filed the deed.

The affidavit lists the names and mailing addresses of sellers and buyers, the legal description, the full price paid, any seller incentives, and the value of personal property included in the price. The assessor uses it for statistical and appraisal analysis and keeps it confidential.

Not every transfer needs one. Exceptions include deeds for nonresidential property, conveyances under a court order, instruments that confirm or correct a recorded deed, transfers between spouses or between parent and child for nominal consideration, and instruments distributing a decedent's estate or trust. The Bernalillo County Assessor posts a Real Property Transfer Declaration Affidavit form and can be reached at 505-222-3700.

sections.h2: Searching records and checking for liens
sections.html:
The clerk's online index covers records from 1978 to the present. You can also use the free public access area at the office. Searches work by legal description, grantor and grantee names, or document number and date.

The clerk's office does not run full real estate searches or full lien checks. Only a title company can do a full search. A paid-off lien also stays on the record until the lienholder files a Release of Lien. If you think an old contractor or judgment lien is long gone, ask for the recorded release now, because the title company will raise the lien at closing otherwise.

Foreclosure and divorce records are not held by the clerk. The Second Judicial District Court keeps them and takes requests online.

Most problems come down to whose name is on the deed. Three situations come up often.

  • A surviving spouse who held the home in joint tenancy can bring a death certificate to the Assessor to update the name. If the property was not held that way, probate court may be needed, and the clerk recommends a lawyer.
  • If the Assessor asks for proof of ownership, give it a copy of the recorded deed or real estate contract, which you can get from the clerk.
  • A lien that was paid but never released remains a cloud on title.

Any of these can slow a closing, and a cash buyer who closes as-is still wants a clean chain of title. Sort them out with a title company before you list.

The Bernalillo County Treasurer page covers tax due at closing, and our Bernalillo County property tax guide covers the Assessor and the tax calendar.

sections.h2: Step by step: recording the deed when you sell
sections.html:
The order below is how a typical sale moves through the clerk's office.

  1. The title company, escrow officer or attorney drafts the deed with the full legal description.
  2. You sign in front of a notary, who adds a seal and expiration date if there is one.
  3. The original, the $25 fee and, if mailing, a stamped return envelope go to the Recording and Filing department, or the title company submits it through an eRecording vendor.
  4. Within 30 days of the clerk's filing date, a residential sale also needs the affidavit filed with the Assessor.
  5. Ask for a certified copy if the buyer's lender or your own records call for one.

faqs.q: How much does it cost to record a deed in Bernalillo County?
faqs.a: It costs $25 per document for up to 10 entries, and another $25 for each additional group of 10 or fewer. The clerk accepts all payment methods except American Express.

faqs.q: Does Bernalillo County charge a transfer tax on deeds?
faqs.a: The clerk's fee schedule lists recording and copy fees only, with no transfer tax line. Closing costs from a title or escrow company are separate.

faqs.q: Do I need the original deed to record it?
faqs.a: Yes. The clerk needs the original, signed and notarized, with the full legal description. If you only have a record copy, a certified copy can be accepted, and the clerk will scan the original and return it.

faqs.q: Can I record a Bernalillo County deed by mail?
faqs.a: Yes. Mail the original, the $25 fee and a stamped return envelope to Bernalillo County Clerk's Office, Attn: Recording and Filing, P.O. Box 542, Albuquerque, NM 87103-0542.

faqs.q: What do I file with the Assessor after selling a house?
faqs.a: For residential property, an affidavit must be filed with the county assessor within 30 days of the date the clerk filed the deed, under section 7-38-12.1 NMSA 1978. Some transfers are exempt.
